system_level_rules: Prioritize Waite for image symbolism, Pollack for system logic, and Gray for classic teaching consensus.
Major Arcana describe archetypal or destiny-weighted processes; Minor Arcana describe day-to-day expression of those forces.
Suit tells you the life domain; number tells you the stage of development; rank tells you how that energy is personified.
When cards repeat a suit, the reading is concentrated in that domain. When numbers repeat across suits, a structural theme is repeating in different areas of life.
Cards are relational: read same-number echoes, elemental tensions, and sequential movement before treating meanings as isolated keywords.
Wands and Pentacles often form a fire-earth tension between inspiration and practicality; Cups and Swords often form a water-air tension between feeling and analysis.
Aces are opportunities, not guarantees. Tens are full consequences, not always happy endings.
Pages announce or begin learning; Knights intensify; Queens deepen and contain; Kings direct and stabilize.
A Major next to a Minor often explains why the smaller event matters; several Majors together indicate a reading driven by larger life transitions.
Card dignity is modified by neighboring cards: supportive cards help expression, challenging cards show cost, pressure, or distortion.

wands.domain: will, vitality, creativity, confidence, initiative, enterprise
wands.shadow: impulsiveness, ego inflation, burnout, conflict for its own sake
wands.logic: Wands show how life-force wants to move. In progression they run from spark, vision, and expansion into victory, pressure, burden, then embodied leadership in the courts.

cups.domain: emotion, attachment, intuition, imagination, relationship, receptivity
cups.shadow: dependency, fantasy, emotional excess, avoidance, sentimentality
cups.logic: Cups show how feeling binds, nourishes, idealizes, grieves, and matures. Their sequence moves from emotional opening into attachment, disappointment, healing, and emotional sovereignty.

swords.domain: mind, speech, truth, analysis, conflict, decision, mental pressure
swords.shadow: overthinking, cruelty, alienation, anxiety, self-defeat, distortion
swords.logic: Swords show what the mind cuts apart and clarifies. Their sequence moves from idea and decision into conflict, strategy, restriction, crisis, and finally lucid authority.

pentacles.domain: body, work, money, health, craft, stability, material manifestation
pentacles.logic: Pentacles show how value becomes tangible. Their sequence moves from seed and exchange into craft, possession, hardship, reciprocity, cultivation, fruition, and legacy.

reversal_logic.core_rule: Reversals are modeled as altered energy states, not automatic opposites.
modes: blocked: the card's function is obstructed or not yet available
internalized: the energy is real but operating inwardly, privately, or psychologically
delayed: the process has started but is not fully expressed in time or form
misdirected: the energy is active but pointed at the wrong target or used badly
excessive_or_deficient: the card overcompensates or underfunctions instead of balancing
application_rules: Majors reversed usually indicate a lesson resisted, deferred, or inwardly activated.
Minors reversed usually show the suit and number pattern breaking down in practical life.
Courts reversed often describe distorted relational style, immature embodiment, or a difficult person dynamic.
Context still governs: supportive surrounding cards can show a reversal being processed rather than simply failing.

relationship_rules.similar_cards: Similar cards share either structural stage, archetypal charge, or a closely allied mode of expression. For pips this is weighted toward same-number resonance in non-opposite suits; for courts it is same-rank resonance; for majors it is thematic kinship.
relationship_rules.contrasting_cards: Contrasting cards are not enemies; they show corrective, opposing, or tension-bearing energies. For minors this is modeled through elemental opposition and opposite developmental stage inside the same suit. For majors it is hand-curated thematic counterforce.
relationship_rules.transitional_cards: Transitional cards show sequence logic. Majors follow the Fool's Journey in a cyclical loop. Minors follow Ace through Ten, then Page, Knight, Queen, King, then cycle back to Ace.
relationship_rules.reading_use: When a card appears with its similar cards, the theme is reinforced. When it appears with contrasting cards, interpretation should look for friction, compensation, or course correction. Transitional cards identify what stage is ending and what stage is emerging.

minor_arcana.ace_to_ten: Read the minors as a developmental arc inside each suit: Ace is the pure seed, Two tests balance, Three expands, Four stabilizes, Five disrupts, Six restores or harmonizes, Seven defends or strategizes, Eight intensifies through motion or discipline, Nine culminates, and Ten shows completion, saturation, or burden.
minor_arcana.ten_to_court: After Ten, the energy becomes personified. The courts show how the suit is learned, pursued, embodied, and governed in human character.
minor_arcana.cross_suit_pattern: Cards with the same number across suits share structural logic but express it through different elements. For example, all Fives destabilize, but Wands fight, Cups grieve, Swords fracture, and Pentacles suffer materially.

upright.summary: Open potential seeking experience.
upright.detailed:
The Fool is Major Arcana zero: not a deficit but a deliberate placement outside the numbered sequence. In the Rider–Waite–Smith image the figure is not lost; they are mid-step toward the cliff, carrying only what fits in a small bundle—experience not yet sorted into story. That posture is the card’s core claim: life can begin again before you have a plan, a reputation, or proof. The teaching is less “be careless” than “recognize the threshold where willingness matters more than certainty.”

Waite’s details reward close reading. The white rose often reads as purity of motive or untested intention; the dog can be warning, loyalty, or the small voice of consequence nipping at the heel; the sun behind carries the sense that the step is illuminated even when the ground ahead is not shown. Together they frame innocence as active: you step because something in you says forward, not because the path has been verified.

In practice, upright Fool commonly marks a new chapter, a first move, travel, study, a leap of faith, or permission to try without guaranteeing outcome. It pairs well with cards that supply structure (Emperor, Hierophant) as tension: freedom meeting order. With The Magician, the contrast is instructive—the Magician gathers tools and names powers; the Fool moves before the naming. Either can follow the other in a life narrative; the Fool emphasizes the uncommitted edge before skill consolidates.

Pollack and Gray’s teaching line stresses the Fool’s Journey: this card is the entry point the rest of the majors answer. So when it dominates a reading, ask what is being entered, what is being left unnamed, and whether the seeker is choosing openness or only avoiding the work of choice. Genuine Fool-energy includes curiosity and proportion; it does not require ignoring real risk—it asks whether the risk serves growth or only postpones engagement.

reversed.summary: Recklessness, drift, fear of commitment, or a blocked beginning.
reversed.detailed:
Reversed, the same threshold energy misfires. One common pattern is the blocked beginning: the person circles the edge of a decision, rehearses openings, and never commits—so potential stays hypothetical. Another is drift without curiosity—motion without orientation, where “keeping options open” becomes a way never to be held accountable to any path.

A sharper shadow is recklessness that is not the Fool’s faith but refusal of consequence: impulse, chronic lateness to responsibility, or thrill-seeking framed as freedom. The dog at the heel can read as ignored warning; the cliff as damage that was visible beforehand. Here reversals borrow from the tradition of “blocked, internalized, or misdirected” energy: the archetype is present but expressed as immaturity, fear, or sabotage rather than as chosen innocence.

Useful questions for reversed Fool: Is there a real first step being avoided? Is risk being taken without preparation where preparation is owed? Is someone calling chaos “spirituality” to dodge contracts, sobriety, or follow-through? Answering those usually clarifies whether the reversal points to fear, to excess, or to a necessary pause before any leap.
